full_text:
Falcons legend Matt Ryan has returned to the franchise as its president of football operations, a role created specifically for him. Mike Stewart / Associated Press
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — Matt Ryan was long drawn to a calling, one that still beckons ever so gently.
Or maybe, a decade since his MVP season as the Atlanta Falcons quarterback and a week removed from downhill mountain biking with his three boys in Jackson Hole, Wyo., such a beckoning wasn’t gentle at all. Essentially out of necessity, the Falcons’ 41-year-old president of football was ripping passes Thursday during a handful of individual periods in the team’s second practice of training camp.
Quarterbacks Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. were unavailable to practice , so Ryan jumped out of the proverbial phonebooth and lent a hand. And a back.
“My back was killing me when I came back last week,” Ryan said with a mix of levity and humility from his new office overlooking the Falcons’ practice field. “I’m thinking I’m like 20 years old, and I’m good to go down this (mountain).
“So we might need a little help throwing just in some of these individual drills. I’m like, ‘My back’s killing me, guys!’ In a normal space where my back wasn’t bothering me, I’d say, yeah, it’s nice to scratch that itch a little bit and go out there and throw. But the last couple days, I’ve been grinning (through the pain).”
Ryan’s evolved calling, the one in his actual job description, has been a bit more appropriate for this chapter of his life. Falcons owner Arthur Blank redesigned the organization’s leadership structure following the 2025 season, its eighth in a row out of the playoffs, and hired Ryan on Jan. 10 to take charge of the football operations, while collaborating with Greg Beadles, who succeeded Rich McKay as the president and CEO on the business side. After a consulting firm determined the Falcons’ vision was too misaligned, Blank opted to make a necessary change and bring in Ryan.
Ryan was instrumental in the Jan. 17 hiring of coach Kevin Stefanski and the Jan. 29 appointment of general manager Ian Cunningham. Stefanski, a two-time NFL Coach of the Year with the Cleveland Browns, was widely viewed as one of the best offseason candidates. Cunningham, the Chicago Bears assistant general manager since 2022, had been considered one of the top GM candidates in the league for a couple of years.
Despite Ryan’s absence of experience in an executive role, the Falcons had an impressive hiring cycle and are poised to enter a new era, with Ryan once again leading the way.
And to think, this was never part of the plan.
Ryan, the No. 3 pick in the 2008 draft, spent 14 of his 15 NFL seasons with the Falcons, and ranks ninth all-time in passing yards, 10th in touchdowns and seventh in both completions and attempts. He spent his final season with the Indianapolis Colts in 2022 and had been working as a CBS studio analyst in his retirement before Blank stoked a fire within Ryan that he didn’t know he had.
Ryan and his family still live in the Atlanta area, and they’ve remained close with Blank and the organization. So when Blank call on Ryan, the owner strung a unique chord.
“I didn’t have grand aspirations after finishing up playing of kind of getting into this,” Ryan said. “But that’s how life works. You don’t know what’s in front of you.”
Ryan loved his job in TV and imagined he’d be over the moon to do it for another decade. He also enjoyed a friendly work-life balance with set studio hours, and he knew that would be the biggest sacrifice if he returned to competition.
Ryan leaned on a handful of people for advice, including San Francisco 49ers GM John Lynch and Jacksonville Jaguars executive VP of football operations Tony Boselli. Ryan wanted to know how the former players transitioned into the front office. Ryan also soaked up knowledge from CBS teammate Bill Cowher, the longtime Pittsburgh Steelers coach, to get a feel for constructing a roster and how to lead a successful building.
The more thought Ryan gave it, the more he felt compelled to seize a potentially once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. His wife, Sarah, also recognized Ryan needed to see it through.
“The thing that just kept coming up in my head was like, ‘I think you’re going to regret this if you don’t go for it,’” Ryan recalled. “(Sarah) kind of felt the same way. She’s like, ‘I know you. I know how you’re wired, and I know being involved in this type of way is something, at the end of the day, if you don’t go for it, you might live with regret over that.’ That was the thing that really pushed it over the edge.”
With Ryan on board and 10 teams searching for head coaches, the Falcons operated more swiftly on Stefanski. It was tabbed as the second-best hire of the cycle, according to The Athletic ’s poll of executives and coaches around the league.
Stefanski was the first Browns coach since Marty Schottenheimer in the 1980s to guide the team to the playoffs more than once. Though they lost more than they won in his other four seasons, the Browns’ most glaring issues stemmed from roster construction and salary cap management with quarterback Deshaun Watson. With a cleaner slate and potentially Stefanski’s most offensively gifted roster, there’s reason to be optimistic about his potential in Atlanta.
Plus, as the Falcons will face their share of adversity, Ryan was drawn to Stefanski’s experience in navigating such murky waters.
“There’s so much that’s learned through the ups and the downs, so I really view that as a strength of Kevin’s that he’s been through it,” Ryan said. “And he’s been through all of it.”
Stefanski, 44, and Ryan both grew up in the Philadelphia area, and Stefanski’s younger brother competed against Ryan in basketball and ran in similar football circles. While Stefanski and Ryan weren’t close before joining forces with the Falcons, they were at least familiar enough with one another.
Ryan’s presence strengthened the attractiveness of the job, Stefanski said. In prior hiring cycles, candidates privately expressed concern over the Falcons’ ambiguous vision and reporting structure, so Blank’s realignment piqued Stefanski’s interest.
“I was extremely comfortable with the setup here, and obviously, Matt stepping into his new role was a huge part of this for me, understanding who he is, understanding what he’s about as a person,” Stefanski said. “He’s the type of person you want to partner with.”
Ryan also had a close connection to Cunningham. Bears general manager Ryan Poles was Ryan’s college teammate and the best man in his wedding, so Poles’ pair of confidants have hit it off wonderfully.
“I’ve always thought if your personal values align, you tend to see football the same way,” Cunningham said. “Now coming here, it makes complete sense why (Poles) and I connected. Because Matt’s values and similarities in terms of how he views football and how he treats people and what it’s about, it’s all the same. I feel like we’re just aligned across the board.”
Cunningham’s front office roots came with the Philadelphia Eagles and Baltimore Ravens, two of the league’s premier executive branches, and he distinguished his reputation through the Bears’ rebuild. Cunningham, also 41, will carry the same team-building values to the Falcons.
Ryan has maintained a core value since his playing days: TSVR. He used to blast it on the whiteboard, and it stands for “time spent, value received.”
AKA: Work smarter, not harder.
Ryan, like any quarterback, needed to outwork opposing defenses to find his edge as a player, so it might feel natural to cede daylight to the outside world while immersing himself in an endless amount of self-orchestrated assignments.
It’s his first year on the job, after all. There’s no blueprint, no precedent.
And with a first-time GM and a coach out to prove himself all over again, there’s no shortage of motivation in the building. It’s just important to harness that energy.

full_text:
What's the ceiling for Bears tight end Colston Loveland? Quarterback Caleb Williams says, “He can be the best tight end in the league.” Aaron M. Sprecher / Associated Press
Colston Loveland doesn’t need to see it, declining the opportunity to view a 13-second clip of his final catch of an impressive rookie season. Loveland remembers the sequence vividly. Late fourth quarter. Divisional-round playoff game at Soldier Field. Less than two minutes remaining with the Chicago Bears fighting to erase the Los Angeles Rams’ 17-10 lead. And driving.
Eight days earlier, Loveland had put his fingerprints all over the franchise’s first playoff victory in 15 years, contributing eight catches, 137 yards and a crucial 2-point conversion grab to a wild 31-27 comeback win over the Green Bay Packers.
One step closer to the Bears’ ultimate playoff goal, the rookie tight end again had himself ready to be a go-to guy in the clutch. Then came his final play. Strike route from the right slot. Smooth release and a burst into a gap in the Rams’ zone.
Quarterback Caleb Williams’ throw jumped at Loveland, hitting him in stride inside a triangle of defenders. Gain of 18. First down.
But as Loveland went to the ground, his neck whipped. The back of his helmet bounced off the ice-glazed grass. He was dazed, trying to stand up quickly, then lying back down. At the climax of a thrilling playoff showdown, Loveland’s season had just ended. He ambled off the field and was corralled for a concussion evaluation. That’s where he was a few moments later, still inside a blue tent on the Bears sideline with no eyes on the night’s most jaw-dropping moment.
“I didn’t see it,” Loveland said. “I heard it, though.”
Williams to tight end Cole Kmet. Fourth-and-everything. Eighteen seconds left. Touchdown. Tie game. Overtime.
“I just wanted to get back out there and continue to make plays,” Loveland said.
But at the climax of an unforgettable season, he couldn’t. He was ruled out. And when an exhilarating night ended with a dispiriting 20-17 season-ending loss, Chicago was instead left with a bunch of “What ifs?”
What if Loveland had been available for the Bears’ 10 offensive overtime snaps? What if the Bears’ final series of the season had included just one more big play from their talented tight end? What if that drive had snuck inside field goal range rather than ending with crossed wires and a killer interception that led to the Rams’ game-winning drive?
If Loveland felt any temptation to live inside those haunting hypotheticals, he quashed that long ago. The present and future are far too important to live inside the past.
“You just have to accept it,” Loveland said. “Accept it and move on. I wish I had been out there. Obviously. But I know I can’t go back and change it.”
“What if” has given way to “What’s next?”
As the Bears move forward, immersed in training camp and hell-bent on returning to the postseason, Loveland knows he will be asked to carry a heavier load.
Following his 58-catch, 713-yard, six-touchdown season, Williams has become one of Loveland’s top endorsers, setting the highest bar for where their journey can go. After the first practice of camp last week, the Bears quarterback lauded Loveland for his route-running polish, massive catch radius and versatility.
By Friday, the duo seemed totally in sync, connecting for a 14-yard touchdown during an end-of-half two-minute period after earlier offering the day’s most impressive highlight: a Williams touch pass with Loveland making a leaping grab over the top of linebacker Devin Bush.
“He can be the best tight end in the league,” Williams said.
The Bears intend to feature Loveland both as a dynamic pass catcher and as a rapidly improving run blocker. In the quest to more heavily lean into two- and three-tight-end sets, Loveland understands the vision of coach Ben Johnson and appreciates the presence of veteran Kmet and rookie Sam Roush in his position room.
“Having athletic, versatile tight ends like we have, it throws defenses off,” Loveland said. “You just have the potential at all times to create mismatches and capitalize. It’s super tricky. We’re in a good spot as far as that goes.”
The Bears also remain in a good spot with Loveland’s Type-A mentality. As productive and encouraging as his first NFL season was, Loveland has taken it upon himself to raise the bar.
“It’s watching the tape,” he said, “and knowing (the performance) was good for a rookie, but it’s not going to be good enough for a second-year or third-year guy.”
For example, he has identified opportunities to be more aggressive and commanding in run blocking.
“(Maybe) it’s like a stalemate or I’m just kind of hanging on,” Loveland said. “Our runner’s not getting touched or whatever. I’m doing my job, technically. But it’s not good enough to put on tape. I think you need to put dominant, really good stuff on tape — really dominating someone, moving someone. That’s the next step.”
If Loveland’s rookie season was an orientation to the intensity of the NFL, it also offered an introduction to the talented quarterback (Williams) he hopes to be playing with for years to come; to the astute head coach (Johnson) who will be designing plays for him for the foreseeable future; to the city (Chicago) that is his new home and pumps with football passion.
In Williams, Loveland noted, he has a leader willing to throw his body around, a quarterback with special grit in the clutch and a partner he can ideally unite with well into the 2030s.
“Caleb is so talented,” Loveland said. “But he is also so passionate about this. He cares so much. And you see it regularly; that he’d do anything to get that next win. How would you not want to ride with a guy like that and catch footballs from someone like that?”
Similarly, how would Loveland not want to ride behind a head coach like Johnson, who creates purpose within every day for everybody?
“Just super intense,” Loveland said. “And one of the most detailed people I have ever been around. That, to me, speaks volumes about how he wants his operation run. And seeing firsthand the way he got everyone around him on the same page, it was like, ‘Yeah, this is a guy I want to play for and get behind.’”
And Chicago? A Bears-crazed city whose gusto he watched come alive all last season?
“Super cool to feel that,” Loveland said. “This is football. Everyone should be loving it. Everyone should get that rush of seeing their team win. You appreciate that.”
It all leads Loveland to an easy conclusion. A window of opportunity seems to be wide open. And no matter how disheartening last season’s finish was, there’s a blend of gratitude and purpose pushing him forward.
“Where else would you rather be?” Loveland said.

full_text:
Dexter Lawrence's impact was noticed in the first week of Bengals training camp. Tanner Pearson / Associated Press
CINCINNATI — The Bengals completed four days of practices and used Sunday to rest. The true creation of the 2026 roster starts at 10 a.m. Monday when pads go on for the first time.
The offseason’s urgency was apparent throughout an active first week, with fights and trash talk littering the practice field. Much of that ends up as a viral spike in social media chatter, but it doesn’t amount to any indication of a real trend.
The themes noted throughout the first four practices are aimed at cutting through the clips and reels for the meat and potatoes of what’s actually meaningful from what I’ve seen during these practices.
Let’s pick up where the offseason left off.
Bengals center and captain Ted Karras is 33. He has played in 174 NFL games and is in his 11th training camp across three organizations.
Experiencing the first week of feeling the Bengals’ new defensive line had him reminiscing about the first camp of his career.
“Today felt like going against the 2016 New England defense,” Karras said after Saturday’s session concluded.
Those Patriots went 14-2, led the NFL in scoring defense and won the Super Bowl. Four days spent wrestling 6-foot-5, 350-pound Dexter Lawrence would have anybody comparing it to the toughest assignment of their career.
“This is about as grown-man of a team as I’ve ever been a part of,” Karras said, before shifting the focus to his Herculean daily assignment. “You saw that last period I’m just fighting to the end there. It’s just me and him in the middle. You better bring your f—ing s— going against Dexter Lawrence.”
The Bengals spent the 2026 offseason purchasing a defensive identity. They’ve spent the last four days establishing it.
Each day a different aspect of the new-look front stood out. On day one, the sheer size and depth of the group stood out. Lawrence leads the way, of course, but the collection of athletes, size and physical freaks transformed this group into an All-Off-The-Bus Team.
“The D-line, certainly, the size difference from last year, is the most glaring thing,” Joe Burrow said. “The pocket was a little different today.”
The next day, the power-speed combination of $20 million edge Boye Mafe shone as he exploded around Amarius Mims, forcing Burrow to spike the ball from the pocket and then affecting a pass that turned into an interception of Burrow by Jalen Davis.
Myles Murphy and Cashius Howell then each had moments finding themselves in the quarterback’s grill, flying off the edge of the 3-4 alignment.
The defensive linemen were basking in the afterglow of a Saturday practice they had just wrecked, and offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher immediately made his way to them with high-fives that might as well have been a tip of the cap.
Guard Dalton Risner started listing all the great defensive players he’s faced over the course of his eight NFL seasons, trying to think of the biggest and strongest.
“Don’t get me wrong, in practice you feel (Lawrence’s) strength,” Risner said. “You feel Jonathan Allen’s experience, his twitchiness. You feel TJ Slaton’s fire. You feel all these guys, but it’s nothing you haven’t felt in your career; but for a practice day in and day out, it’s certainly not the most fun.”
None of it looks fun for the offense. What the Bengals put together up front isn’t unprecedented. It’s far too early to tell if it will work in the long run.
However, it sure as heck hasn’t been easy for the offensive line to handle and offers a reminder of the group’s potential.
“It’s a stressful August for me,” Karras said, “but at least I get to pass it off to our opponents come September.”
The first four days have helped dispel any inkling that expansion of the dormant under-center offense during OTAs was merely offseason tinkering.
We’ve seen under-center, under-center with play action, under-center with play action and motion, and packages built off every wrinkle of that.
We still don’t know how serious the implementation will be when the games get real, but we do know the concept of adding that weapon to Burrow’s arsenal has never looked more real.
These allow Pitcher and Zac Taylor to tinker with new packages beyond the standard 11 personnel they have spent the majority of Burrow’s career running as much as any other team.
It offers expansion of the Erick All Jr. role as he looks healthy to an exciting degree coming off double-ACL surgeries and getting hit by a truck in Greece . That’s an exciting twist on 12 personnel that’s gaining momentum. There’s also a chance to dabble in two running backs with Chase Brown’s work training as a receiver growing the idea of using him in a versatile slot subpackage.
The repetition also helps a Bengals offense that, between Dylan Fairchild and Risner, hasn’t had this level of guard play in a decade be able to lean on an under-center run game capable of bringing a new level of explosiveness.
All of these have seen the foundation laid in the first four practices, and the next step will be about how much each specific element evolves when camp gets more physical. Either way, Burrow sounds on board with whatever direction it goes.
“I’m very comfortable (under center),” he said. “I can do whatever is asked of me. I have, and I will. And we haven’t done it quite as much over the last several years, and we’ll see what we evolve into this year. But if that’s what’s needed, that’s what I’ll do.”
Depth at cornerback has been one of the most concerning issues heading toward the season. Starters DJ Turner and Dax Hill were set, but the rest looked up for grabs among a handful of young, unproven or journeymen players.
The hierarchy looks much more established through the first week than the wide-open battle would suggest.
Hill and Turner have been joined by Jalen Davis, as expected, with the starting group (and Davis has shown well, making the most of his opportunity). The second-string group hasn’t changed. Often you’ll see rotations from day to day or even drill to drill in a true competition. Instead, DJ Ivey and Tacario Davis outside and Ja’Sir Taylor in the slot have taken nearly all the second-team reps. Josh Newton remains in the same doghouse that kept his snaps limited down the stretch last season.
Ivey thrived as a third-down tight end stopper last year and will do that again, but the Bengals proved this week they are quite open to the idea of the 2023 seventh-rounder doing more.
“I definitely feel like there is opportunity out there,” Ivey said. “Any chance I get, I’m taking the opportunity to make plays and show the coaches I’m here to be seen and I’m here to make an impact.”
In December of Ivey’s rookie season, he tore an ACL, and rehab caused him to start the 2024 campaign on the Physically Unable to Perform list. He only played eight games. Last year was his first full season back, and he mostly played on special teams.
Now fully healthy and removed from the ACL injury, he might never have a better chance to prove he can play outside corner than this.
Rookie Tacario Davis is looking to replicate what Ivey did as a rookie three years ago. Ivey splashed as a surprising star of that camp. Davis playing well wouldn’t be a surprise considering he’s a third-round pick out of Washington, but it would go a long way in making everyone feel better about depth in the secondary.
He got his hands on a pass breakup for the first time in camp on Saturday and kept a quiet humility during his first taste of progress.
“To get to where I want to go and be one of the greatest, you got to keep stacking days,” Davis said. “It’s a good thing, trending in the right direction, but keep moving forward. Instead of making the PBU, make the great play and get the interception.”

OXNARD, Calif. — Gary Downs played six seasons as a running back in the NFL. He can identify a talented football player. But at 6 years old?

full_text:
The Cowboys took Caleb Downs with the 11th overall pick and so far everyone in training camp has liked what they've seen from him. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
OXNARD, Calif. — Gary Downs played six seasons as a running back in the NFL. He can identify a talented football player. But at 6 years old?
That’s the age his son, Dallas Cowboys rookie safety Caleb Downs, was when his father knew he was a special player. The first-grader scored 46 touchdowns in a 10-game season. In the championship game, he finished with 313 rushing yards and seven touchdowns on offense and 15 tackles on defense.
“We would always say, ‘When you get older, it’s going to get harder,’” Gary recalled. “But as he got older, he just kept getting better and better. He plays the best against the best people. … He’s just different. He just rises to the occasion, his work ethic, his IQ.
“When he puts his mind to something, he does it. That’s a gift. That’s a talent. If he says one day I want to be like Jerry Jones and own a team, don’t bet against him.”
Gary remembers Caleb coming home from elementary school and watching film. He would also study YouTube videos of the NFL’s greatest safeties, like Ed Reed, Brian Dawkins, Troy Polamalu and Ronnie Lott.
“He’s a learner,” Gary said. “He studies the Hall of Famers because that’s where he wants to be at.”
Gary witnessed the same dedication when it came to Caleb’s schoolwork, from a young age and through college. While at Ohio State, Caleb studied business with an emphasis on real estate.
“We set up meetings with real estate (companies) and developers,” Gary said. “And after all those meetings, they would say, ‘I’ve never been around a young person that could go and sit and study or watch for five or six hours.’ He literally could do that, because he wanted to, and he would never get tired. They said, ‘You’re probably tired. You’re probably bored?’
“Nope. If there was a developer right now that said, ‘Caleb, I want to show you some development in Frisco (Texas),’ he would be like, ‘Let’s go.’ And then after an hour or two, they would be like, ‘You’re probably tired.’ No. He’s locked in because he’s interested. His ability to focus (is exceptional).”
That type of praise has followed Downs throughout his football career. Nick Saban, arguably the greatest coach in college football history, was only with him for one season, but he considers Downs to be one of the best people and players he has coached during his 51-year career.
The Cowboys are starting to see why.
Monday marks the first time Dallas will be in full pads for a training camp practice. Downs will be easily noticed. During their work in organized team activities, minicamp and the first week of training camp, Downs has been moved all over the defense. He’s the chess piece that new defensive coordinator Christian Parker has been utilizing to help as a nickel cornerback but also a traditional safety. One play he could be asked to make a run stop like a linebacker and the next he’s defending a top wide receiver or tight end in the passing game.
“They shouldn’t call it nickel, they ought to call it Downs,” Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said Saturday on NFL Network. “Really. He was built for that.”
Parker has been spending extra time with Downs after practice. It’s clear the Cowboys knew when they traded up to draft him 11th overall in April that they could put a lot on his plate. So much so that Downs is one of four defenders who will be getting work during camp wearing the green dot, the helmet radio that receives the play calls from Parker. That’s a role usually reserved for veteran players.
“He’s a young guy that I respect,” Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott said. “He’s a reason that this is going to be one of our best rookie classes. And he’s just going to continue to grow. He takes a lot of pride in being the first pick of the Cowboys and takes a lot of pride in having to step into a defense that everybody was talking about that has to get better.”
The Cowboys are coming off a season where they had what many consider to be the worst defense in franchise history. Downs isn’t going to turn it all around alone, but he doesn’t shy away from the expectations.
“To be dominant,” Downs said of his expectations for the defense. “That’s what I’ve thought about with every defense I’ve been on. And we have the talent to do it, to dominate every offense that we go against.”
The importance of the nickel cornerback has increased in recent years. Jones acknowledged as much going into this year’s draft, sharing that the Cowboys would not have allowed veteran cornerback Jourdan Lewis to leave in free agency had they known how essential that role would become.
Downs is the ideal fit in a league where so many star wide receivers are moved around the formation, including into the slot. Downs has the ability to stay with them at any position.
“That’s what makes these offenses great, when you can move these (top wide receivers) in and out,” Prescott said. “And so if you don’t have a guy that can travel with them, if you don’t have a guy that can match up and play that, you’re putting yourself in a bind. And (Downs) not only has to travel and get inside (when) that guy goes inside, but he also has to stop the run. And so to have a guy that can do that, to be versatile, but more importantly, physical, that’s what makes great defenses great.
“You need a guy in there that can slow down that star receiver when he moves inside, but yet fill the B-gap, the C-gap or wherever he needs to and hold the integrity of the defense.”
The Cowboys have a pair of outstanding wide receivers they can move around in CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Downs’ reps against them should help him greatly during the season.
Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer has praised Downs for his ability to not make the same mistake twice. After being beaten on a route by Lamb in the spring, Schottenheimer used it as a teaching moment in front of the entire team. The route was run again recently in training camp, and Downs was in position to take Lamb away.
“His ability to adjust is very mature,” Lamb said. “He understands where his help is. In minicamp, that was his first time in that defense. He wasn’t really understanding what was going on. But now he plays to his help, he plays to his strength and it shows. The guy’s phenomenal. He’s a great football player. I can’t wait to see what he does on Sundays.”
Nothing about Downs seems like a rookie. He carries himself like a veteran on and off the field, never appearing uncomfortable.
When he arrived at the Cowboys’ headquarters, The Star, the day after he was drafted, a fan told him he hopes he’s the next Ed Reed.
“I’m just gonna be me,” Downs calmly responded. “I’m just gonna be Caleb Downs.”
When asked last week about how high his expectations are for himself, Downs simply said: “That’s for me to know and y’all to find out.”
The jump from high school to college was not an issue. Downs was the best freshman in college football while at Alabama. He then transferred to Ohio State and picked right up where he left off as one of the nation’s top defensive backs, earning All-American honors both seasons and winning a national championship in 2024. Many experts believe he was the best all-around player in this year’s draft. The jump from college to pro looks like it might be just as smooth.
“He’s as sharp of a young guy as I’ve ever seen,” Prescott said. “It starts with his mentality and his approach to the game. It’s who he is. Obviously you can see it on the football field. You see it any moment that football is being talked about, whether it’s in the meetings or whether it’s a walk-through or it’s at practice. But just to spend time around the guy outside of football, whether it’s playing golf or just hanging out, shooting a commercial with him, that’s who he is. And that is contagious.”

full_text:
Colts tight end Tyler Warren delivered an impressive rookie season, collecting 76 receptions for 817 yards and four TDs. Can he top those totals in Year 2? Robert Goddin / Getty Images
WESTFIELD, Ind. — There was no celebration. Heck, there was barely even a reaction. After Tyler Warren broke to the end zone and high-pointed a pass from quarterback Daniel Jones for a touchdown, the fans inside the Indianapolis Colts’ indoor practice facility Saturday erupted with joy. Their top tight end had just made one of the most memorable plays of training camp, yet his only response was to simply high-five a few of his teammates and return to the huddle.
Warren’s nonchalant response belies how hard he works, according to his coaches and teammates, and what he’s capable of with the ball in his hands. As promising as his rookie campaign was, it was only a preview, many of them say. This year could be even better as he enters his second season in coach Shane Steichen’s offense.
“I think that (continuity) is really important with getting the same coaches back and having a lot of the same players back,” Warren said last week on The Fan Morning Show. “… We’re not installing (new plays) every day. We’re kind of just going back over stuff. There will be new installs and stuff like that, but I think it’s important we have that foundation we’ve already built everything on and just kind of building off of it.”
Tyler. Warren. 🙌 pic.twitter.com/JE477GOb1D
— Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 2, 2026
Warren totaled 76 catches for 817 yards and four TDs during a promising rookie season in 2025. He finished with the fourth-most receiving yards by a tight end in a single season in Colts history, trailing only Hall of Famer John Mackey and Ring of Honor member Dallas Clark.
Warren’s production took a noticeable dip when Jones fractured his left fibula and ultimately tore his right Achilles tendon. The second-year tight end, however, was part of a slew of Colts pass catchers who recently joined Jones on a trip to Florida so that they could practice together in the lead up to training camp. Their unofficial minicamp also served as a progress report for Jones, whom all his teammates praised for his remarkable Achilles rehab.
Jones, just eight months removed from surgery, took every first-team rep during the Colts’ four consecutive practices to start training camp. After a couple of up-and-down moments as he reacclimated to 11-on-11 drills, he looked his sharpest Saturday. Jones finished 14-of-17 passing as the Colts focused heavily on executing in the red zone.
“He looks like he never got hurt,” tight end Mo Alie-Cox said. “You see, he’s throwing dimes left and right on the field, getting out the pocket scrambling and different things like that. I think his confidence is building more and more every day, and when we put the pads on (Monday), I think it’ll just take it to another level.”
Quenton Nelson, who’s blocked for several quarterbacks throughout his now nine-year tenure with the franchise, said he’s thrilled to have Jones back in the saddle as they prepare for their second season together. Throughout the first week of training camp, Nelson was often one of the first players to hype Jones up after leading the offense down the field.
“He’s been incredible,” Nelson said of Jones on Saturday. “He’s back like he never left.”
Nelson was much more interested in discussing his teammates to conclude the first week of training camp than he was about his contract situation. The star left guard is entering the last year of his four-year, $80 million deal. He said in the spring he would defer to his agent regarding any potential negotiations, and his hands-off approach hasn’t changed.
“I haven’t had any discussions. That’s not up to me,” Nelson said. “I’m just really thankful to be here. Excited for this year, and (I) love this team, love my teammates.”
The Colts drafted Nelson sixth overall in 2018, and he’s become arguably the greatest offensive lineman in franchise history. Nelson is an eight-time Pro Bowler and six-time All Pro.
The last time he signed an extension, the deal was agreed to the night before the Colts’ season opener in 2022. The Falcons recently signed their star left guard, Matthew Bergeron, to a four-year, $96 million extension that could inform the price point for Nelson’s new deal.
Spencer Shrader and Blake Grupe squared off Friday in the first kicking competition of training camp. Grupe made all six of his field goal attempts from 33, 37, 41, 45, 50 and 55 yards. Meanwhile, Shrader was 5-of-6, missing his 50-yard attempt wide left. This was only the second public kicking competition of the offseason, with Grupe drilling all five of his field goal attempts during OTAs in the spring and Shrader missing two.
Shrader suffered a season-ending knee injury last October that derailed a very promising campaign. He drilled 13 of his 14 field goal attempts in five games. In Shrader’s absence, the Colts eventually turned to Grupe, who was cut midseason by the New Orleans Saints but bounced back tremendously in Indy. After missing eight field goal attempts in 11 games last year with the Saints, Grupe was a perfect 11-of-11 on field goals with the Colts, highlighted by a 60-yarder.
“We expect there to be a little bit of rust and some inconsistency since he hadn’t kicked for eight months,” Colts special teams coordinator Brian Mason said of Shrader last week. “I think he’s cleaned up some of those things throughout the summer. It continues to get better. … Grupe, since he’s been here in practice, in the season, in OTAs, he’s been highly consistent.”
Rookie linebacker CJ Allen was removed from the physically unable to perform list and made his camp debut Friday. The second-round pick missed the first two days of camp due to a calf strain that he said was caused by overtraining.
“I think a got a little ahead of myself,” Allen said after his return. “Probably should’ve shut it down that day, went home, got some treatment. But decided to get another (workout) in and had a small little tweak.”
Allen was never worried that he’d be sidelined long, and he was immediately inserted into the Colts’ starting defense. Defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo has been experimenting with Allen wearing the green dot in his helmet, meaning he’ll relay the defensive calls to the rest of his unit. The former Georgia star held those responsibilities in college and joked that he’s only faced one issue since transitioning to the NFL.
“I’m from Georgia, so I got like a little southern twang. So, I gotta really enunciate my words,” Allen said through a grin. “But nah, just making sure we’re on the same page, being a communicator. The guys kind of respect that.”

full_text:
So far, Brock Bowers is delivering a big play per day in camp. Ian Maule / Getty Images
HENDERSON, Nev. — The Las Vegas Raiders are nearing the conclusion of what head coach Klint Kubiak called the “underwear Olympics” portion of training camp. This week, the team will have its first padded practice and real football can commence.
But the early days of camp are not for nothing. The Raiders put in a lot of high-intensity work during their initial four practices. Much could be gleaned about the makeup of the team — specifically where players stack up within the roster.
The stock of several Raiders shifted — some for better, others for worse — during the opening week of training camp. Things certainly will change again after the pads come on, but here’s a look at a few players who stood out so far:
The star tight end has been the standout of camp so far, hands down. Bowers has made at least one big play in each practice, and seemingly in every team period. He’s had his way with every defender he’s gone up against.
Bowers is dominating on crossing routes — a staple of Kubiak’s offense. A highlight of the team’s second practice came when he beat his man across the field and extended to catch a Kirk Cousins pass on the sideline, stretching out while keeping his feet in bounds. Bowers caught a pair of touchdowns from Cousins on crossing routes during their third practice. And while lined up on the perimeter on Sunday, he beat top corner Eric Stokes with an outside release before crossing his face and separating with speed for a big gain. It was the kind of play that’s difficult for most NFL wide receivers.
“He’s a bigger body, and he’s smooth at the top of the route,” safeties coach Matt Robinson said. “All you need is a little bit of space, and if you put it on Brock, he’s gonna catch it. It’s a challenge for us.”
Bowers was hindered last year by a nagging knee injury suffered in the season opener. But he is back healthy and looks ready to produce, like he did in his record-setting rookie year, as the focal point of this Kubiak scheme.
Kubiak challenged Masses before the team broke from mandatory minicamp in June, asking publicly if he could replicate his strong performance in the offseason program during training camp. So far, the rookie corner has risen to the occasion.
Masses has earned reps with the first team opposite Stokes in every practice so far and has held his own. While it comes as a surprise that a fifth-rounder has run so much with the first unit, receiver Tre Tucker said he’s known Masses’ talent from early on.
“I was watching rookie minicamp, just looking at the guys, and I was like, ‘Who is 35, man? Like he’s over everyone,’” Tucker said. “And then actually getting to go against him, I can see it.”
Masses saw fewer opportunities on Sunday than he did in past practices, as second-year corner Darien Porter took most first-team reps during team periods. But if he continues on his early-camp trajectory, Masses could be a legitimate contender for a starting spot this season.
Another late-round rookie who’s put veterans on notice this camp is Benson. The sixth-round draft pick has found good chemistry with No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza so far, earning him more opportunities as camp has gone on.
Benson’s best highlight was for naught, as he made an impressive play on a back-shoulder throw from Mendoza in the end zone but was ruled out of bounds. Still, he’s had several big catches with the second unit and repped some with the ones as well. And off the field, veteran receiver Jalen Nailor said the rookie is conducting himself in the right way.
“He’s a young kid, he has a ways to go, but he’s asking the right questions,” Nailor said. “He wants to be better, he wants to play, he wants to be on this team and he wants to show himself.”
Benson has shown a lot for a player of his draft status early in camp. He has an uphill battle against Tucker, Nailor and the other veteran receivers for playing time, but more may come if he continues to impress.
The Raiders have a plethora of interior defensive linemen with experience, but Hemingway seems to be making headway amongst them.
The second-year defensive tackle has received plenty of first-team reps alongside Adam Butler and Jonah Laulu. He’s succeeded in those chances, making a few solid run stops and tipping a Cousins pass at the line.
Defensive line coach Rob Leonard said Hemingway has become more mature and consistent this offseason, adding that he’s incorporated much of Maxx Crosby’s routine into his own.
“It’s been fun to watch him develop as a man, as a player, and now he’s got to carry it over to pads,” Leonard said.
Hemingway played in just nine games as a rookie and didn’t log a single start, but he did have three sacks in the Raiders’ final two games. His strong play has continued into training camp.
McCoy hasn’t been challenging for a starting spot just yet in camp, as all of his reps have come with the second and third units. But McCoy’s ability to compete in each of the team’s practices so far is considered a win.
“He’s been available … which is a really positive start,” Kubiak said. “To see him out there getting as much work as he’s getting has been excellent.”
Kubiak has called McCoy a “moving target” as the team manages a knee issue that caused him to fall to the fourth round in April’s draft. He was held out of most of OTAs and all of mandatory minicamp as the team figured out a plan. While he’s been limited in training camp, McCoy has gotten snaps in almost every team period — a positive sign for his health moving forward.
The rookie has had some hiccups on the field; he got beat by Shedrick Jackson on a go ball on Sunday, forcing him to commit a holding penalty to avoid giving up a touchdown. But he’s also shown signs of his elite talent, such as when he broke up a slant to E.J. Williams earlier in the practice.
McCoy just being available has him headed in the right direction. The more snaps he gets, the more his skills will begin to show.
Stukes hasn’t struggled in camp. He’s been sound in his assignments, as he was during the offseason program. But the second-round pick has earned fewer opportunities than might be expected.
Stukes has yet to receive a first-team snap in any competitive period. That strays from his role this offseason, where he got chances with the ones at both safety and nickel. Veterans Taron Johnson and Jeremy Chinn missed some of those practices, however, allowing Stukes to step in. With both suited up for all training camp sessions, the rookie has been relegated to second string. He will have to show something once the pads come on to crack the rotation.
Glaze had a rough second season in silver and black. His 10 sacks and 48 pressures allowed were second-most league-wide in 2025, according to TruMedia. Some of those struggles have followed into Year 3.
The right tackle has had trouble with the Raiders’ pass rushers, as Crosby and Malcolm Koonce have had sacks against him. Pressure has noticeably been stronger from Glaze’s side as compared to Kolton Miller on the left. Crosby also got by Glaze on Sunday for a run stop of Ashton Jeanty.
While Glaze’s performance doesn’t matter much until he’s in full pads, the Raiders did show the first signs of concern on Sunday. Third-round rookie Trey Zuhn III played exclusively at right tackle with the second unit after spending the first three practices at center and right guard. Glaze has received every snap with the first team so far, but if he doesn’t look good when contact starts, Zuhn or others could make it a competition.
Meredith had been mixing in with Zuhn at center with the second team to start camp. Zuhn bumping outside on Sunday should have allowed the veteran to claim all of the rookie’s snaps, but Meredith was instead relegated to the threes, and Will Putnam served as the second-team center.

full_text:
Rookie first-round pick Caleb Banks is healthy and has looked impressive in the early going at Vikings training camp. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Saturday’s training camp practice showcased the Minnesota Vikings’ vision for 2026. Improved quarterback play, combined with an enhanced run game, should make for an improved offense. That generates intrigue because the team still boasts one of the NFL’s most menacing defenses.
Kyler Murray, in particular, looked sharp. He found superstar receiver Justin Jefferson on a crossing route, one of the staples of coach Kevin O’Connell’s system. He decisively distributed the ball on quicker concepts. Meanwhile, the offense utilized a bevy of formations, inspiring the possibility of dynamism and misdirection.
But one preseason practice does not guarantee a successful season — and it doesn’t come with any declarations about the starting quarterback. The Vikings and O’Connell designed this competition to produce consistency over days and weeks. Leaving that subject for later in the week, we thought it would be worthwhile to evaluate some other areas of the roster.
Who is standing out? Who has struggled? Here is our first edition of training camp risers and fallers:
Let’s begin with a brief history lesson. The Vikings drafted 28 players from 2022 to 2025, and only four of them have become full-time starters for the franchise. None have participated in a Pro Bowl. Kicker Will Reichard and receiver Jordan Addison came the closest.
The lack of success in the draft forced Minnesota to build its roster through free agency, which is suboptimal and unsustainable for any NFL team. This contributed to general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah’s ouster.
The 2026 NFL Draft became the responsibility of Vikings lifer Rob Brzezinski . Minnesota’s longtime negotiator and salary-cap expert selected nine players this spring with massive input from college scouting director Mike Sholiton’s staff and the team’s coaches.
Early returns look promising. First-round pick Caleb Banks responded from left foot surgery and is already mixing in with the starters. Second-round linebacker Jake Golday tipped a pass Saturday, evoking shades of edge rusher Andrew Van Ginkel.
There has been positivity from the later-round picks, too. Assistant head coach Frank Smith spent some time after Saturday’s practice reviewing techniques with fullback Max Bredeson. Cornerback Chuck Demmings blanketed Jefferson and deflected a pass. Safety Jakobe Thomas continues to show up in all areas of Brian Flores’ defense, and undrafted safety Jacob Thomas tends to play right alongside him.
It’s easy to make too much of the start of training camp. But it’s a good sign that so many of these players have already shown promise.
The Vikings’ rushing attack took a major step forward in 2025. It may not have felt that way, but the numbers are telling.
Minnesota ranked 12th in the NFL in yards per carry, sixth in rushing success rate, fifth in explosive rush rate and 14th in EPA per rush. A heavy personnel shift affected these statistics. The decisiveness and cutback ability of Jordan Mason helped, too.
To O’Connell’s credit, the Vikings are seeking further growth. They swapped offensive line coach Chris Kuper for Keith Carter. Beginning in the spring, Carter set a higher standard for physical training. The Vikings also brought in Smith, the Miami Dolphins’ former offensive coordinator, who brings insights from a team and system that were at the tip of the spear in recent seasons.
Miami’s scheme featured interesting motions, quarterback ball-handling techniques and multiple strategies to attack the edge of the defense. Former Dolphins fullback Alec Ingold, who followed former Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel to the Los Angeles Chargers, became a fixer in the run-blocking phase.
Bredeson’s early involvement evokes many of these possibilities. Add in the potential of Murray’s dual-threat skill set, and you can conceptualize the Vikings’ expectations.
Both of the Vikings’ starting tight ends, T.J. Hockenson and Josh Oliver, have missed games in recent years due to injury. This means depth will be important.
Bartholomew, a sixth-round pick in 2025 out of Pittsburgh, missed his entire rookie season due to a back injury. But his pass-catching reliability stood out during the first week of camp. Bartholomew adjusted to throws down the seam. He secured completions in the red zone. Padded practices will provide more data on his run-blocking ceiling, but he is already making a case for a back-end role.
Because the Vikings drafted two interior defenders in 2026, Rodriguez lost some shine. But he should still play an important role. So far in camp, when the starters have trotted out onto the field and the team sets up with a five-man front, Rodriguez joins Jalen Redmond on the unit.
The story still resembles a fable. Rodriguez went from athlete at Southwestern Assemblies of God University to defensive lineman at Texas A&M-Commerce. The Vikings found him and drafted him in the seventh round. He developed enough to play 461 snaps last season, and the recent infusion of youth does not mean the 25-year-old has become a finished product.
In the past two training camps, McGlothern made enough plays on the ball to pique the team’s interest. He even flashed in some spare 2024 snaps when matched up with then-Chicago Bears wideout Keenan Allen. The locker room adores him. Neither the front office nor coaching staff questioned his commitment in recent years. But through the first week, McGlothern received few snaps with the premier groups of players.
It also doesn’t help that another undrafted cornerback, Zemaiah Vaughn, has earned meaningful opportunities. Demmings’ athleticism is eye-catching, too. Depending on health and how many cornerbacks the Vikings keep on the 53-man roster, McGlothern may face an uphill climb.
The Vikings ranked eighth in the league in special teams DVOA last year. Reichard’s efficiency played a major role in the success. Former punter Ryan Wright reached a palatable floor as well. The team’s 23 special teams penalties were the seventh most in the NFL, but special teams coordinator Matt Daniels often attributed the flags to youth.
Assessing this phase isn’t easy because the Vikings have kept the team-oriented special teams work to a minimum thus far. Reichard hasn’t kicked in front of the media. Punters Johnny Hekker and Brett Thorson haven’t booted the ball or held for Reichard, either.
Golday shifted from the traditional linebacker position to the edge Saturday. His comfort there offers some conviction about what the Vikings have behind Dallas Turner and Van Ginkel, but the rest of the possible replacements come with questions.
Bo Richter, Chaz Chambliss and Tyler Batty are all undrafted players trying to carve out bigger roles. Even though the Vikings have high hopes for Turner, and their defense doesn’t hinge on one pass rusher taking over games, acquiring a more veteran pass-rushing replacement still makes sense.
Three years ago, Pace was the belle of the training camp ball. Flores tossed him into snaps with the starters, and Pace ducked his way underneath blockers with reckless abandon. He’s still capable and can cause major problems for running backs in pass protection. His 5-foot-10 frame can serve as an advantage when he’s weaving his way through attempted pullers and blockers.
His positives, however, often come with positioning in the wrong gaps and a lack of reliability in coverage. That’s why his defensive snaps have diminished each year. He played 706 defensive snaps in 2023 and 323 in 2025. Bringing in versatile defender Jamal Adams means infusing the roster with another blitz-capable body who may push Pace for one of the team’s final roster spots.

The Athletic has live coverage of NFL training camp .
WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The goal for the New York Giants never was to have quarterback Jaxson Dart operating at his peak at the start of August. It was understood that it was going to be a process as Dart acclimated to a new offense. The expected growing pains have been evident in the first four practices of training camp.
Former coach Brian Daboll made Dart’s transition to the NFL as comfortable as possible by importing many of the passing concepts from the Ole Miss playbook into the Giants’ offense. That enabled Dart to enjoy success as a rookie, but there’s a ceiling on a college-style offense in the NFL. So, new coach John Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy have challenged Dart to run a more traditional offense.
That means an emphasis on playing under center to facilitate what’s expected to be a run-heavy attack. That’s a major adjustment for Dart, who was in the shotgun on 79.9 percent of his snaps as a rookie. For comparison, Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was in the shotgun on 67.1 percent of his snaps last season.
Dart said he feels comfortable with the footwork changes he’s had to make, but those aren’t the only differences. He’s turning his back to the defense more and going through more reads than in the RPO-heavy offense he ran last season. That could explain why the offense has looked disjointed early in camp.
Part of the problem for the offense has been a dominant pass rush. The edge rushers, particularly Abdul Carter , have been consistently disruptive. And there have been breakdowns in protection as defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has dialed up more exotic pressures as camp has progressed.
Dart’s ability to make plays out of structure was proven last season, and he has shown those abilities at times during camp. He has been at his best on throws to the second level, with many of the route combinations in Nagy’s offense springing receivers open on deep crossers.
Harbaugh acknowledged they’re still figuring out what will work best for this group. That’s what camp is for, and that’s why Harbaugh was more forgiving of a mistake like the interception Dart threw to defensive tackle Darius Alexander during a two-minute drive at the end of Friday’s practice.
Harbaugh has sung Dart’s praises despite the uneven start to camp.
“You can’t even imagine how much there is for a quarterback to operate with, especially in a new offense,” Harbaugh said. “He’s done an outstanding job. There’s so much on his plate. He’s pushing the envelope. He’s also competing at the same time. He’s a fiery guy. I’m very impressed.”
Cornerback is the most intriguing position on the roster. Paulson Adebo and Greg Newsome have been the top two corners throughout the offseason, but Deonte Banks and Colton Hood are lurking.
Adebo is in the second year of the three-year, $54 million contract he signed last offseason. That investment was made before Harbaugh arrived, and Adebo likely didn’t endear himself to the football-obsessed coach by skipping the start of the voluntary offseason program. Adebo’s shaky start to camp could open the door for a surprise shakeup to the lineup.
The Giants gave Newsome, a 2021 first-round pick by the Browns, a one-year, $8 million contract to fill the void created by Cor’Dale Flott’s free-agent departure. Newsome has split time between the slot and the perimeter throughout his career, and he has mixed into the slot occasionally early in camp.
Banks fits the profile of a talented underachiever who could be revived by a new coaching staff. The 2023 first-round pick has had a strong offseason, which has earned him some first-team reps in camp.
The Giants used a second-round pick on Hood this year, so he’s clearly a big piece of the future. The question is how quickly he’ll work into the lineup.
Uncertainty at slot corner adds a layer of unpredictability. Dru Phillips has been the starting nickel corner for the past two seasons, but he has been splitting time with versatile former Raven Ar’Darius Washington. Newsome could start outside, in the slot or split time between the spots, depending on how the secondary comes together. It will be fascinating to see how it unfolds throughout the preseason.
A balanced, scrappy athlete who can attach himself to receivers; likely an early starter.
The biggest story from the start of camp has been wide receiver Malik Nabers’ presence on the field. Even when Nabers avoided the physically unable to perform (PUP) list to start camp, it wasn’t known how much he would do as he completes his recovery from a torn ACL and torn meniscus.
Nabers participated in individual drills and ran routes on air (no defenders) in the first two practices. He sat out on Friday as the team carefully manages his workload before returning to action on Saturday with the same participation level as the first two practices.
Nabers has looked good, with Harbaugh saying, “He’s generally on schedule.” The Giants are taking it day-to-day, determining Nabers’ workload based on how he feels each day. With six weeks until the season opener against the Cowboys, it’s hard to imagine Nabers not being ready barring a setback.
All of the focus on the returns of Nabers and running back Cam Skattebo has overshadowed the importance of left tackle Andrew Thomas’ health. Thomas underwent ankle surgeries after the 2020 and 2021 seasons and then spent last offseason recovering from the Lisfranc foot injury that limited him to six games in 2024.
The Lisfranc recovery lingered into the start of last season, and Thomas missed the first two games. He then played 13 straight games, returning to his All-Pro form, before being shut down with a minor hamstring injury for the final two weeks of the season.
The Giants managed Thomas’ workload during the spring as part of a maintenance plan for a player with an extensive injury history. He has taken nearly every rep during team periods during camp, with Marcus Mbow and Josh Ezeudu only stepping in for the occasional snap.
The approach led Thomas to declare on the second day of camp that, “This is the best I’ve felt in a long time.” Nabers and Skattebo are important, and a case can always be made for the quarterback as a team’s most valuable player. But the impact of Thomas’ absence in recent seasons has made the case that he’s the team’s most indispensable player . Having him healthy entering this season is a major development.
Wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. delivered a vintage catch in Saturday’s practice. Beckham ran a skinny post in the red zone and made a toe-tapping touchdown catch in the back of the end zone from Jameis Winston.
The highlight was a long time coming for Beckham, who has had a very quiet start to camp in his comeback bid after sitting out last season. The 33-year-old can still run, and his hands remain strong, but he has failed to make plays in team periods.
As a backup who doesn’t play special teams, Beckham will need to show enough value as a receiver to claim a roster spot. There’s time for him to raise his performance, but the start to camp has been underwhelming aside from the one throwback grab. Beckham will face competition from a veteran like Braxton Berrios, who adds value as a returner and has been a productive slot receiver early in camp.

full_text:
Dylan Buell / Getty Images
Sometime in the fall of 2020, a wooden throne with a velvet-lined seat, seven feet high and 200 pounds, sold for $75 on Facebook Marketplace.
The buyer was a football coach in Idaho.
Each Friday, the throne followed the Skyline High School football team in Idaho Falls. A parent would load it onto a pickup truck and deliver it to the sideline for games. A player forcing a turnover would be feted like a king: gold chain (with a thick wooden paw and “Grizz” insignia across the middle) draped around his neck. He’d then climb onto that wooden throne — the “Turnover Throne” — and be lifted by celebratory teammates.
The throne followed Skyline throughout its state championship run in 2020, and it was present for the title game in 2021, too. However, by the end of that game, the throne had a human-sized dent in the side of it.
The damaged throne still stands. Years later and 2,200 miles east, the kid responsible for the damage shrugs his shoulders.
“I broke it, I guess,” Kenyon Sadiq says.
Standing outside the New York Jets’ facility in northeast New Jersey, Sadiq, the Jets’ first-round rookie tight end, looks around and smiles. He appreciates the sounds of silence — or, at least, how it sounds tucked into a quiet area, when construction at the facility isn’t roaring. He prefers peace.
When he found out the Jets drafted him, the prospect of living in Manhattan stressed him out — it’s a long way from the woods of southeast Idaho. When he first arrived in Florham Park, he breathed a sigh of relief.
Silence soothes him, but the tranquility also animates him. Through a life lived in nature, much of it spent fishing with his late grandfather, he learned to turn the volume down in his brain. Most people exercise to fast-paced music. Sadiq listens to slow jams when he works out.
And the way he plays football, he might as well be wearing noise-canceling headphones. He rarely hears the sounds of a crowd, even the deafening noise of Oregon’s raucous Autzen Stadium, where he played his collegiate home games. He says there are moments when all he sees is the man in front of him, or the ball as he leaps for a catch or the end zone as he runs toward it.
“What Kenyon would explain to me,” his mother, Heather Pledger, says, “is the game slows down in his head. So he could feel himself in the air and then catch the ball. Like, the ball would come in slow motion to him.”
His preparation is so intense, so thorough, that all he needs is a task — beat the man in front of you on a route, catch the ball when it’s thrown to you, make defenders miss once it’s in your hands. Or, block the man in front of you and don’t stop until he’s on the ground.
Pledger recalled moments that made her think of the movie “The Blind Side,” when Michael Oher blocked someone through the back of the end zone and over a fence at the end of a play. Sadiq did something like that more than once. His mom would ask him: Where’d you go, son? Did you forget the game was still going on?
“You tell Kenyon to finish, he’s gonna finish,” she says. “Whatever that means.”
That’s what he did in that 2021 state title game. He took a Sandpoint High defensive back and blocked him through Skyline’s sideline, and then he kept going.
He finally stopped. He’d blocked the kid into the throne. It tipped over.
“He broke it!” his mom says, laughing.
The image was fitting. A throne symbolizes power, and with that comes fame and adulation. Sadiq never had interest in any of that.
McCammon, Idaho, is a two-stoplight town with a population in triple digits. The area it covers is so small that a bike ride across the entire town takes about 10 minutes. For locals, “going into town” means driving 30 minutes away to Pocatello to get groceries at Walmart. A few years ago, McCammon got its first-ever Family Dollar, which was a big deal.
In this small stretch of land, Terry Pledger, Sadiq’s maternal grandfather, was beloved. An Idaho boy from Pocatello, Pledger was a three-sport high school star who stayed home to start a family with Alaina, the love of his life, rather than pursue dreams of playing baseball professionally.
As an offensive lineman, he had offers to play college football, too. Instead, he worked at Kraft for a time, then became a police officer, a coach and a girls basketball referee. He pushed his daughter to find her passion. Heather danced, ran track, played volleyball and basketball. Terry had her playing baseball too; she was the only girl on the team.
When Pledger looks at her son, she sees her dad: his athleticism, determination, kindness, intellect, love of nature — his essence. Even his hands, which she calls an “exact” replica of her father’s. Perhaps that’s why grandfather and grandson got along so well.
“He saw a lot of himself in my son,” she says.
There were stretches when Heather, with Kenyon’s father out of the picture, was working as many as three jobs at a time — running restaurants, working at dental offices, graveyard shifts at the hospital, gigs at the local horse track, among others — for her three kids: Kenyon, his sister, Daisha, and his brother, Mikhi.
Kenyon learned to do his own laundry at 5, and he and his siblings sometimes had to cook for themselves. For stretches, they’d move back in with her parents until she could get back on her feet.
There wasn’t a whole lot to do in town — and Kenyon, she says, was “very rambunctious,” a “daredevil.” Heather was constantly buying him new shoes because he would “run holes in all of them.”
Kenyon wanted to keep up with his sister, who was 14 months older than him, so he was already riding a bike without training wheels at 2. He’d come home sometimes, bloodied, and it was always: “Kenyon, what did you do now? We’ve got to get stitches because we told you not to do wheelies on your bike.”
Heather signed him up for sports, though soccer and baseball bored him. He did karate. He was a Boy Scout, earning every badge. However, it was football that satiated him. And it started when his grandpa put a ball in his hands for the first time, at 6.
“He’d always be saying cringy things like: Be the hammer, not the nail,” Sadiq says. “He was making sure I wasn’t a little wimp out there.”
Sadiq was 16, making himself breakfast, finishing schoolwork on the computer and then, around noon, going to the local gym to work out with his friends while other kids his age were at school.
His workout buddies were in their 50s and 60s, doctors and dentists on their afternoon breaks. After working out, he’d head home, make a protein shake, finish more schoolwork and then head to football practice. When his mom was picking up groceries, he’d give her a list of vitamins and amino acids.
COVID-19 sent students online in 2020, and Sadiq wanted to keep it that way. High school — the school part, at least — wasn’t for him. The NFL was his goal, so Sadiq pitched his mom on letting him join an online schooling program based in Idaho: It would allow him to devote more time to training and remove some of the typical distractions of teenage life. He wasn’t especially interested in socializing or partying. He wanted to work.
“I feel like I matured a bit faster than some of the kids that I was around,” Sadiq says. “So just being around them all day felt like a waste of time.”
Those old gym friends — he still talks to some of them — helped educate him on fitness and weight training. The exercise became a form of therapy, like fishing on a lake with his grandpa. He’d put on his headphones, listen to ’90s R&B and clear his mind. Sadiq found his center at 16, wise beyond his years.
The scholarship offers poured in, but not immediately. It takes a little longer for word to travel from Idaho to the big schools, and many college coaches are unwilling to make the trip.
However, Scott Berger, Sadiq’s high school coach, knew he had someone special. Sadiq transferred to Skyline after his freshman year. His previous coaches tried playing him at defensive end, but Sadiq wanted to…

full_text:
Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers' offense struggled during a playoff loss to the Houston Texans. Joe Sargent / Getty
Read our exclusive interview with Aaron Rodgers
The Pittsburgh Steelers’ playoff loss to the Houston Texans in January was decisive enough that Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers spent the final 2 minutes and 39 seconds on the bench, comprehensive enough that the visiting Texans turned the ball over three times — and still recorded the biggest margin of victory in the postseason’s opening weekend.
“I don’t feel like we ever got the momentum on our side, honestly,” Rodgers said after the 30-6 defeat . “We had a lot of chances … a lot of opportunities. Didn’t make the most out of hardly any of them.”
Unsaid at the time: Rodgers had been so sick before the game that teammates and coaches had expressed hope he could mimic Michael Jordan’s iconic “Flu Game” in the 1997 NBA Finals.
Though few people beyond the Steelers’ sideline knew it, the 42-year-old quarterback had been felled by flu-like symptoms in the hours leading up to the game, making the experience even more miserable.
“I wasn’t feeling good, and I actually came over to the team hotel, and they sent me home — probably because I was pale and looked like s—,” Rodgers revealed in an interview with The Athletic following Saturday’s training camp practice at St. Vincent College.
During the conversation, Rodgers, whose symptoms included fever and vomiting, made a point of insisting that he’d recovered by kickoff, crediting the Texans’ ferocious defense for an epic effort.
Yes, he sucked it up. Clearly, however, the timing sucked. For all the legendary things the four-time MVP has done in his two-plus-decade career, the illness contributed to a nightmarish playoff exit. Rodgers finished 17 of 33 for 146 yards against the Texans’ top-ranked defense, throwing one interception — a pick six late in the fourth quarter — and losing one of his two fumbles. It left him with a 50.8 passer rating, the worst of his postseason career and the second worst of his 17 starts for Pittsburgh.
“He’s definitely downplaying it,” said former Steelers offensive coordinator Arthur Smith, who now serves in a similar role at Ohio State. “There was never a question he was gonna play, and he’s never one to complain, but he looked terrible (before the game).”
The Steelers didn’t mention Rodgers’ illness after their loss, and the focus soon turned to coach Mike Tomlin, whose departure after 19 seasons became public the next day.
Tomlin was typically blunt on the night of the playoff loss: “When you don’t get it done, words are cheap,” he said. “It’s about what you do or don’t do…. People talk too much in our business. You either do or you don’t.”
Had the Steelers won, though, Rodgers’ poor health would have added another entry to his drama-filled list of greatest moments.

full_text:
Enrique Cruz Jr. was the 49ers' final pick of the draft in April. Jeff Chiu / Associated Press
SANTA CLARA, Calif. — When backup left tackle Vederian Lowe limped off the field with a high ankle sprain midway through the San Francisco 49ers’ first training camp practice last week, any number of players could have jumped in to replace him.
There was Austen Pleasants, who was in the No. 2 role last year and started a Week 18 game against the Seattle Seahawks. Brandon Parker has been in the league since 2018, the past two years as a member of San Francisco’s practice squad. Even International Pathway Program player Isaac Alarcon was a good candidate considering he’s in his third 49ers training camp.
Instead, the least experienced of them all, rookie Enrique Cruz Jr., bounded into the huddle like an eager golden retriever, and the second-team offense didn’t skip a beat.
“Coach, who goes in?” Cruz recalled excitedly asking Chris Foerster. The offensive line coach’s quick response: “You! You go in!”
The sequence ended up being a good way to get rid of Day 1 jitters, Cruz said. And it offered a glimpse at one of the rookie’s top qualities: He isn’t shy.
“He has an infectious personality,” Cruz’s high school coach, Nick Hildreth, said. “He’s fun, he’s so outgoing, he’s so happy to be there. I’ve never seen him where he’s negative toward anybody, ever.”
Cruz is very much a project. He was the last of the 49ers’ draft picks in April, going late in the fifth round at No. 179. And barring a flurry of injuries at his position, he’s unlikely to see the field this season.
Still, he’s the first true offensive tackle — a college tackle the 49ers intend to keep at that position — they’ve drafted in five years, and his athletic skills compare to those of the team’s most recent left tackles, Joe Staley and Trent Williams. The idea of anyone replacing Williams, a 12-time Pro Bowler who is still going strong at age 38 and plans to play two more seasons, is daunting, but Cruz has skills worth developing.
Kansas' Enrique Cruz Jr.'s impressive Combine continues with a 4.95u
2026 NFL Combine on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dHswaB315X
— NFL (@NFL) March 1, 2026
At 313 pounds, Cruz ran his 40-yard dash in 4.94 seconds and reached nearly 21 mph while doing so. It’s clear in early training camp practices he’s got the foot speed to reach linebackers, on the front and backside of the 49ers’ wide-zone runs.
“He’s got great feet and hands,” right tackle Colton McKivitz said. “He’s gonna have to learn a little bit — our scheme and how he fits in with that. But the talent he has is (apparent).”
Hildreth got his first glimpse of Cruz at an open house for incoming freshmen at Willowbrook High in Villa Park, Ill., which is 20 miles west of Chicago. Hildreth closely followed the area youth leagues and was familiar with the pool of new talent. Cruz’s family, however, had just moved from the city.
“So this kid comes walking in with his mom, and me and my assistant coach did a double take together,” Hildreth recalled. “Because he was not on my radar as an incoming freshman. He was long and gangly but had a good frame to him. You just knew he was going to be a monster.”
Hildreth had strategically placed his table by the entrance and made sure Cruz didn’t slip by. And though the two hit it off right away, there were some early obstacles.
The first was Cruz fancied himself a basketball player. Even after Hildreth convinced him to give football a try, he informed his coach he was a wideout.
“And I’m like, ‘You’re not a wideout,’” Hildreth told Cruz, who grew to 6 feet 5, 252 pounds before his senior season. “We did throw him the ball his senior year. He got the ball in his hands once.”
Another problem was Cruz’s GPA, which fell as low as 1.4. His worst subject? Cruz laughs and admits it was Spanish — funny because his family’s from Puerto Rico and he speaks the language.
“It was a different version of Spanish,” he said. “I’d be at my grandma’s house doing it, and my grandma would tell me it’s wrong, it’s the wrong term because it’s Puerto Rican Spanish and not Spanish Spanish. So it was pretty hard for me to learn.”
The low point came during his sophomore year, just as Cruz was starting to get serious about football. It was something his coach used as leverage. One day that fall, Hildreth informed Cruz he was moving him up to varsity ahead of a pivotal game against a district rival. A trophy was on the line. There was excitement in the air. And Cruz thought he was going to be on the field Friday night with the older boys.
He wasn’t. The move was instead designed to give the then-15-year-old a taste of what it was like to be on the varsity squad and to entice him to lift his grades. That, and a serious sit-down with Hildreth after Cruz’s sophomore season, made an impression.
“And from that day on, every time I saw him in the hallway, it was, ‘Coach! I’m being a scholar today!’” Hildreth said.
Hildreth also convinced Cruz to drop his beloved basketball for wrestling, a sport he’d never tried before but one that would make him a better offensive lineman.
“It’s hard on the ego to be the biggest, baddest kid in the building and then go to the wrestling room and get beat up,” Hildreth said.
Cruz truly took off as a junior. He was tall, powerful, long-limbed, and he could pull and wreak havoc on opposing linebackers. During the playoffs that year, Cruz caused a riot of euphoria on the Willowbrook sideline when he blocked a highly touted opponent out of the back of the end zone and into a snowbank.
“That was the beginning of his coming-out party,” Hildreth said.
By the time he graduated, his GPA was up to 3.0, and he’d gotten a scholarship from Syracuse.
Hildreth essentially told Foerster that story when the 49ers assistant flew to Willowbrook to give Cruz a workout before the draft.
“I told him the kid, when he’s faced adversity — academically, on the field, COVID, all that stuff — he responds,” he said.
Foerster came away impressed. When he pushed Cruz hard during the workout, he responded. So Foerster kept pushing and returned to Santa Clara convinced he’d make a good 49er.
It’s early, of course, but the plan is still on track.
“Enrique’s been a real plus,” Foerster said of the rookie’s first few days of camp. “Everybody in the building’s pleased with him. People come up out of nowhere from all over the building and say, ‘Gosh, that Enrique’s doing a really nice job.’ He’s really professional, really working on it. He has a learning curve, like all the young guys do.
“He’s got a long way to go, but he’s done all the right things to this point.”
